title: The Triplets of Belleville
full_review:
A French grandma sets out to rescue her kidnapped grandson from mobsters in the surreal animated feature �The Triplets of Bellevilleö (Sony Classics). French comic-book artist and filmmaker Sylvian Chomet has crafted a work of visionary brilliance and singularity, both humorous and tender, that defies categorizing. And although this cartoon is definitely adult fare, this visual tour de force offers viewers some of the most inspired animated sequences in recent memory.

Told virtually without dialogue, �Tripletsö uses simple pantomime to achieve a level of emotional nuance rarely attained in live-action performances. Set in the 1950s, Chomet�s kaleidoscope of sights and sounds revolves around Madame Souza, a plump Gallic Granny with a club foot and saucer-sized eyes. She lives on the outskirts of Paris, in the shadow of elevated traintracks, with her melancholy grandson, Champion. To cheer him up she gives the lad a shiny red tricycle, a gift that sparks a vocational epiphany. Years go by and Champion, now a grown man with Popeye calves, is ready for the Tour de France � having been coached by his whistle-tooting grandma.

During the race he is shanghaied, along with two other cyclists, by a pair of geometric gangsters who resemble walking black coffins. They smuggle him aboard a towering wedge-shaped ocean-liner and take him to the megalopolis of Belleville � a city teeming with people so bulbous they look like balloons in Macy�s Thanksgiving Day parade. But Madame Souza and her faithful slobbering hound Bruno take up the chase, tracking him across the storm-tossed sea. Once in Belleville, they enlist the aid of the eponymous triplets, a trio of gangly crones who dress like faded flappers. When not feasting on assorted frog-ka-bobs, the ex-music hall hags perform a cackling cabaret act using household appliances to supply the musical accompaniment � with surprisingly melodious results.

Sounds weird. Don�t let that deter you. �Tripletsö is one of the most audaciously original films in years. Exuding unhinged imaginative brio, the movie elevates animation back to its rightful place among art forms worthy of respect. Chomet draws inspiration from a wide range of sources, resulting in a smorgasbord of high brow and pop-culture influences, paying homage to the cartoons of Tex Avery and the films of Jacque Tati. Chomet buttresses his splendidly off-kilter visuals with an equally effulgent soundtrack � an eclectic patch-quilt of jazz and kitch � celebrating the music of Mozart and Django Reinhardt.

Parents should be warned that this cartoon is not for the kiddies. �Tripletsö is laced with racy images, including a risqu opening cabaret number during which a bare-breasted, albeit animated, Josephine Baker performs a hoochie-coochie routine, as well as fleeting lewdness in the hallways of the squalid brothel where the aged hags live. And while the film contains some gunplay, it is no more violent than the classic Warner Brothers� Loony Tunes.

It is truly amazing what Chomet has accomplished, in regards to characterization, without the use of dialogue. In many ways �Tripletsö owes more of its pedigree to the grand tradition of French mimes and the silent films of Chaplin and Keaton than it does to any animated antecedent. The kooky characters, through rubber-limbed expressionistic exaggerations, are inherently human. And the angular backgrounds are at once both familiar and fantastic� a landscape that alternates between enchanting and nightmarish.

And though it�s a long shot, come Oscar time when they announce best animated film �Finding Nemoö may find himself swimming home empty finned. C�est la vie, Pixar.

Due to stylized violence, fleeting cartoon nudity, minimal mildly crude humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III - adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG - parental guidance suggested.
